Part 1 of 7

North vs. South

CORE OBJECTIVE

Core Objective 1: Identify the respective advantages of the North and South as the Civil War began, and explain how they affected the military strategies of the Union and the Confederacy.

IN MY WORDS: What did each side have going for it when the war began?

Reading AWho Had the Advantage?

The population count was about 22 million in the Union (some 400,000 of whom were enslaved African Americans) to 9 million in the Confederacy (of whom about 3.5 million were enslaved).

An even greater asset for the North was its superior industrial development. The Southern states produced just 7 percent of the nation’s manufactured goods. The Union states generated 97 percent of the firearms and 96 percent of the railroad equipment.

The Confederates, however, had major geographic and emotional advantages: they could fight on their own territory in defense of their homeland. In warfare, it is usually easier to defend than to attack . . . Many Confederate leaders thought that if they could hold out long enough, disgruntled Northern voters might convince Lincoln and Congress to end the war.

Word help: asset = something helpful · superior = better · manufactured goods = things made in factories · disgruntled = unhappy and angry

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 14, “Mobilizing Forces in the North and South” (Regional Advantages).

Reading BTwo War Plans

First, the Army of the Potomac, the main Union army, would defend Washington, D.C., and exert constant pressure on the Confederate capital at Richmond.

Second, the Federal navy’s blockade of Southern ports would cut off the Confederacy’s access to foreign goods and weapons. The third component called for other Union armies to divide the Confederacy by pushing south along the crucial inland water routes: the Mississippi, Tennessee, and Cumberland Rivers. This so-called Anaconda Plan was intended to slowly trap and crush the Southern resistance, like an anaconda snake strangling its prey.

The Confederate plan was simpler. If the Union forces could be stalemated and the war prolonged, as Jefferson Davis and others hoped, then the British or French, desperate for cotton from the South, might be persuaded to join the cause.

Word help: blockade = ships stopping goods from going in or out · component = part · anaconda = a huge snake that squeezes its prey · exert = put on · stalemated = stuck with no winner · prolonged = made longer

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 14, “Mobilizing Forces in the North and South” (The Union’s “Anaconda” Plan; Confederate Strategy) (p. 577).

Part 2 of 7

Emancipation

CORE OBJECTIVE

Core Objective 2: Evaluate Abraham Lincoln’s decision to issue the Emancipation Proclamation and its impact on the war.

IN MY WORDS: Why did Lincoln free enslaved people in the Confederacy, and how did it change the war?

Reading CAntietam and the Emancipation Proclamation

The Battle of Antietam revived sagging Northern morale and dashed the Confederacy’s hopes of forging military alliances with Great Britain and France. It also convinced Lincoln to transform the war from an effort to restore the Union to a crusade to end slavery.

On September 22, 1862, five days after the Battle of Antietam, President Lincoln issued the preliminary Emancipation Proclamation, which changed the course of history. . . . The Emancipation Proclamation was not based on ideas of racial equality or abstract ideals of human dignity. It was, according to Lincoln, a “military necessity” and therefore a legitimate use of presidential “war powers.”

He justified the Emancipation Proclamation (1863) as a military necessity because it would deprive the South of its captive labor force.

Word help: morale = spirit, confidence · alliances = partners in war · crusade = a fight for a cause · preliminary = first, early · deprive = take away from · captive labor force = enslaved workers

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 14, “Emancipation” (Antietam: A Turning Point; Emancipation Proclamation) (p. 593). Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 14, “Reviewing the Core Objectives”.

Reading DFreeing Themselves and Fighting

Large numbers of enslaved people freed themselves by escaping to Union camps and working for the army. In July 1862, with the Militia Act, Congress had declared that formerly enslaved people (contrabands) could enlist in the Union army too.

More than 180,000 Black men enlisted in the army, most of them formerly enslaved and 80 percent from Southern states. In the navy, African Americans accounted for about a fourth of all enlistments.

Word help: enlist = join the military · contrabands = enslaved people who escaped to Union lines · accounted for = made up

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 14, “Reviewing the Core Objectives”. Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 14, “Emancipation” (Black Soldiers and Sailors).

Source QA Black Union Soldier Writes Home, 1864 (Primary Source)

Jacob Christy was a free Black man from Pennsylvania who fought as a Union soldier. He wrote this in a letter home in 1864.

“I do really think that it’s God’s will that this war Shall not end till the Colored people get their rights,” . . . “and I shall die a trying for our rights so that others that are born hereafter may live and enjoy a happy life.”

Word help: Colored people = a term used then for African Americans · a trying = trying · hereafter = in the future

Jacob Christy, letter, 1864, as quoted in Norton, Ch. 14, “Emancipation” (Black Soldiers and Sailors).

Source Q. What did Christy believe the war should not end without? What was he willing to do for it?

Point of view. Lincoln called emancipation a “military necessity.” Christy saw the war as a fight for rights. Why might a Black soldier see the war differently from the president?

PicturePresident Lincoln, Writing the Proclamation of Freedom (1863)

David Gilmour Blythe made this painting in 1863. Norton says it shows the positive (Union) view of Lincoln’s role in issuing the Emancipation Proclamation. (It is a primary source.)

What to look for: Flag = the United States · Scales on the wall = justice, weighing what is fair · Piles of papers and books = laws, documents, and study · Lincoln’s plain shirt = a hard-working, ordinary man

David Gilmour Blythe, President Lincoln, Writing the Proclamation of Freedom, 1863. In Norton, Ch. 14, “Emancipation,” Visual Explorations: “Union and Confederate Views of the Emancipation Proclamation.” Primary source.

Picture evidence. Name two things you see around Lincoln. How do they make him look like a hero to Union supporters?

Part 3 of 7

Home Fronts, Turning Points, and Victory

CORE OBJECTIVES

Core Objective 3: Analyze how the war affected social and economic life in the North and South.

Core Objective 4: Describe the military turning points in 1863 and 1864 that ultimately led to the Confederacy’s defeat.

Core Objective 5: Explain how the Civil War changed the nation.

IN MY WORDS: How did the war change life at home, and how did the Union finally win?

Reading ETwo Economies at War

In addition, a Homestead Act (1862) granted 160 acres of public land to each settler who agreed to work the land for five years. . . . the National Banking Act (1863), which created national banks that could issue paper money that would be accepted across the country.

Compared to the Union’s, Confederate efforts to finance the war were a disaster. . . . In the cash-poor South, however, the government printed so much paper money that it caused severe inflation of consumer prices, which led to even more personal trauma and civil unrest.

Word help: granted = gave · issue = print and hand out · finance = pay for · inflation = prices going up fast · civil unrest = riots and protests

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 14, “The War behind the Lines” (Wartime Government; Confederate Finances).

Reading FTurning Points and the Road to Appomattox

The Union victories at the Battle of Vicksburg and the Battle of Gettysburg in July 1863 were a major turning point of the war. With the capture of Vicksburg, Union forces cut the Confederacy in two . . . General Robert E. Lee and the Army of Northern Virginia lost a third of its troops after the defeat at Gettysburg.

In 1864, Lincoln placed General Ulysses S. Grant in charge of the Union’s war efforts . . . General William Tecumseh Sherman’s “March to the Sea” (1864) resulted in the Union’s conquest of Georgia and South Carolina.

Sherman’s successes helped propel Lincoln to victory in the election of 1864. After that, Southern resistance wilted, forcing Lee to surrender his army to General Grant at Appomattox Court House in April 1865.

Word help: turning point = the moment things change direction · conquest = taking over by force · propel = push forward · wilted = grew weak · surrender = give up

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 14, “Reviewing the Core Objectives”.

Reading GA Transformed Nation

Northern victory restored the Union—and transformed it. What Lincoln called the “monstrous injustice” of slavery had been abolished, and a key issue had been resolved: no state had the right to divorce itself from the Union.

Upon ratification by three-fourths of the reunited states, the Thirteenth Amendment became law eight months after the war ended, on December 18, 1865.

Not only did the power of the federal government increase, but the center of political and economic power shifted away from the South and the planter class.

Word help: restored = brought back · abolished = ended · divorce itself = leave · ratification = official approval · planter class = rich plantation owners

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 14, “A Transformational War” (The Union Preserved; Thirteenth Amendment). Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 14, “Reviewing the Core Objectives”.

Part 4 of 7

Rebuilding the South

CORE OBJECTIVES

Core Objective 6: Identify the federal government’s major challenges in reconstructing the South after the Civil War.

Core Objective 7: Describe how and why the federal government’s Reconstruction policies changed over time.

IN MY WORDS: What problems did the government face after the war, and how did Congress’s plan differ from Johnson’s?

Reading HBig Questions after the War

With the defeat of the Confederacy and the passage of the Thirteenth Amendment, the federal government had to develop policies and procedures to address a number of difficult questions: What was the status of the defeated states, and how would they be reintegrated into the nation’s political life? What would be the political status of the formerly enslaved people, and what would the federal government do to integrate them into the nation’s social and economic fabric?

Yet what did freedom mean for the formerly enslaved, most of whom had no land, no home, no food, no paying job, and no education?

Word help: status = position or condition · reintegrated = brought back in · integrate = include fully · fabric = the way society fits together

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 15, “Reviewing the Core Objectives”. Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 15, “Battles over Political Reconstruction” (The Freedmen’s Bureau) (p. 633).

Reading IThe Freedmen’s Bureau and the Black Codes

The Bureau also provided the now-free African Americans with medical care, clothing, shelter, and food. By 1868, the Bureau had distributed more than 20 million meals. In addition, it assisted formerly enslaved people in seeking justice in courts, managed abandoned lands, and helped formalize marriages and find relatives.

Southern Whites resisted and established Black codes to restrict the lives of formerly enslaved people.

The codes also barred African Americans from voting, serving on juries, or testifying against Whites. . . . Any Black people not apprenticed or employed by January 1866 would be jailed as “vagrants.”

Word help: Bureau = a government office (the Freedmen’s Bureau) · formalize = make official · restrict = limit · barred = blocked · apprenticed = bound to work for someone · vagrants = people with no job or home

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 15, “Battles over Political Reconstruction” (The Freedmen’s Bureau; Black Codes). Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 15, “Reviewing the Core Objectives”.

Reading JFrom Johnson’s Plan to Congress’s Plan

Abraham Lincoln and his successor, the Southerner Andrew Johnson, preferred the more lenient Presidential Reconstruction Plan for the states of the South. . . . Lincoln’s assassination led Northerners to favor the Radical Republicans, who wanted a more radical plan designed to transform the South’s society and economy.

Congressional Reconstruction responded by stipulating that to reenter the Union, former Confederate states had to ratify the Fourteenth (1866) and Fifteenth (1870) Amendments to the U.S. Constitution to expand and protect the rights of African Americans.

Ultimately, the race riots helped spur the Republican-controlled Congress to pass the Fourteenth Amendment (1866), extending federal civil rights protections to African Americans.

In their place, Congress established military control over ten of the eleven former Confederate states. . . . The Military Reconstruction Act required each former Confederate state to write a new constitution that guaranteed all adult males the right to vote—Black or White, rich or poor, landless or property-owning. . . . The Fifteenth Amendment prohibited states from denying a citizen’s right to vote on grounds of “race, color, or previous condition of servitude.”

Word help: lenient = easy, not strict · race riots = violent attacks on African Americans in Southern cities · assassination = murder of a leader · radical = wanting big change · stipulating = requiring · ratify = officially approve · servitude = slavery

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 15, “Reviewing the Core Objectives”. Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 15, “Battles over Political Reconstruction” (Congress Takes Charge of Reconstruction; Expanding Voting Rights) (p. 646).

Part 5 of 7

Freedom and Its Limits

CORE OBJECTIVE

Core Objective 8: Assess the attitudes of White and Black Southerners toward various Reconstruction programs and requirements.

IN MY WORDS: How did Black and White Southerners each react to Reconstruction?

Reading KThe Quest for Land and Sharecropping

Many freedpeople argued that what they needed most was land. . . . But Andrew Johnson reversed such transfers of property to formerly enslaved people. . . . A formerly enslaved man in Mississippi said that he and others were left with nothing: “no land, no house, not so much as a place to lay our head.”

Other freedpeople participated in a new labor system: sharecropping. It worked like this: Black laborers would rent a portion of land on which to raise crops and then pay the rent by giving the landowner a share of the crop. . . . Over time, however, most sharecroppers, Black and White, found themselves deeply in debt, with little choice but to remain tied to the same discouraging system of dependence that felt much like slavery.

Word help: freedpeople = people freed from slavery · reversed = undid · portion = part · debt = money owed · dependence = needing someone else to survive

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 15, “Black Society under Reconstruction” (The Quest for Land; Sharecropping) (p. 654).

Reading LBlack Leaders and White Violence

New African American voters helped elect nearly 800 Black men—most of them formerly enslaved—as state legislators. . . . There were two Black senators in Congress, Hiram Revels and Blanche K. Bruce, while fourteen Black congressmen served in the U.S. House of Representatives.

Whites continued to use terror, intimidation, and violence to disrupt Black Republican meetings, target Black and White Republican leaders for beatings or killings, and prevent Black people from exercising their political rights. . . . Secretive terrorist groups—including the Ku Klux Klan, the Knights of the White Camelia, the White Line, and the White League—emerged to resist Radical Reconstruction and to harass, intimidate, torture, and even kill African Americans.

Word help: legislators = lawmakers · intimidation = scaring people to control them · exercising = using · harass = bother and threaten

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 15, “Black Society under Reconstruction” (African American Political Leadership; Southern Violence) (p. 656).

Part 6 of 7

The End of Reconstruction

CORE OBJECTIVES

Core Objective 9: Analyze the political and economic factors that helped end Reconstruction in 1877.

Core Objective 10: Explain the significance of Reconstruction to the nation’s future.

IN MY WORDS: Why did Reconstruction end in 1877, and why does it still matter?

Reading MPanic and a Deal

The resulting Panic of 1873 caused a deep economic depression. Tens of thousands of businesses closed, 3 million workers lost jobs, and those with jobs saw their wages slashed.

Scandals during the Grant administration . . . eroded Northern support for Reconstruction.

In the Compromise of 1877, Democrats agreed to the election of Republican Rutherford B. Hayes, who removed federal troops from the South.

By 1877, many White Americans were no longer willing to pay the price to protect the newly won rights of African Americans. . . . The news led a South Carolina African American citizen to dread his future. “I am an unprotected freedman. O God save the Colored People.”

Word help: depression = a long, very bad time for the economy · slashed = cut a lot · scandals = shameful acts by leaders · eroded = wore away · dread = fear

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 15, “The Grant Administration” (Financial Panic; The End of Reconstruction) (p. 664). Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 15, “Reviewing the Core Objectives”.

Reading NWhy Reconstruction Still Matters

Southern state governments quickly renewed long-standing patterns of discrimination against African Americans, but the Fourteenth and Fifteenth Amendments remained enshrined in the Constitution, creating the essential constitutional foundation for future advances in civil rights. These amendments give the federal government responsibility for ensuring equal treatment and political equality within the states, a role it would increasingly assume to this day.

Word help: renewed = started again · discrimination = unfair treatment · enshrined = kept safe, permanent · foundation = base · assume = take on

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 15, “Reviewing the Core Objectives”.

Unprotected. Why did the South Carolina man in Reading M call himself “an unprotected freedman” after 1877?
